title: Al-Wakil, the Trustee
hookLine: the Trustee, the one you hand things over to, after doing your part (Tirmidhi)

cards: A man comes to see the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. He gets off his camel, and stops. Should he tie the camel up, and then trust God to keep it?
Or leave it loose, and trust God, full stop? If he ties it, is he trusting less? If he doesn't, is he being a fool?

The question has modern versions: the exam you study for or don't, the door you lock or leave. How much is on you, and how much do you hand over? The camel came up in passing eight days ago, with ar-Razzaq.
Today it gets the whole lesson, and a very short answer. Today: tawakkul.

teach.b: The answer, in the collection of at-Tirmidhi: tie it, and trust. Both, in that order. Tawakkul is the word for that trust, from the same root as today's name, al-Wakil, the Trustee.

In ordinary Arabic, a wakil is the person you hand your affairs to: an agent, a representative, the one who handles it when you can't. Calling God al-Wakil means he is the One you hand things over to.
But the hadith sets the order. First you do your part. Tie the rope.
Study for the test. See the doctor. Then you let go of the outcome, because it was never fully in your hands.
Not doing nothing. Doing what's yours, and letting the rest rest. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's words: "And whosoever putteth his trust in Allah, He will suffice him."
It sets the same order in Al 'Imran.
The Prophet is told to consult his companions in the matter, and then, once he has decided, to put his trust in God; the verse adds that God loves those who trust. Consult, decide, then trust.
And there's a phrase many Muslims say when things are heavy: hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil.
God is enough for us, and he is the best Trustee.

In the Qur'an, believers say it when they're told an army has gathered against them, and the next verse says they came back with grace from God. It's said in the face of the threat, not instead of facing it.

how: Muslims describe tawakkul as taking every reasonable step and then relying on God for the outcome, and many say hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil in hard moments.

o: giving up and letting fate decide
trusting God so you need not act
trust in God after doing your own part

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: the one who handles your affairs

s: tawakkul means leaving everything to God and doing nothing
the hadith says tie the camel first. do your part, then trust.
the Qur'an tells the Prophet to trust first and consult afterward
3:159 runs the other way: consult them, and when you have decided, then trust.
tawakkul and al-Wakil share one root
a wakil is the one you hand things over to.

games.q: you have come to see the Prophet. your camel is standing there. you want to trust God completely. what do you do with the camel?
o: leave it loose. trust means not tying it.
games.why: tie it, and trust: the Prophet's answer in at-Tirmidhi. doing your part is part of the trust.

practice: Think of one thing you're worried about, and ask honestly: what's the rope I can tie, one email, one call, one appointment, one conversation?
Name it, then look at what's left, the part that isn't yours to control, and picture setting it down. If you pray, you can say hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil; if not, just breathe out, and let it rest.

wordCard.voice: Tawakkul. Trust in God, from the same root as al-Wakil, the Trustee: do your part, then hand over the rest. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: trust, reliance on God. the same root as al-Wakil, the Trustee.

carryVoice: Your line: tie the camel, then trust. Your part first, and the rest is handed over. That's day two hundred fifty-three.

sources.q: And whosoever putteth his trust in Allah, He will suffice him.
